title: Consumer groups and rebalancing
goal: By the end, you can explain how a group of consumers shares a topic's partitions, hand a partition's bookmark over cleanly when it moves, say what each of the three ways of moving partitions stops, and pick the settings that decide when a member is thrown out of its group.
opening:
Picture the last day of the month. Card payments pour into Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages and lets other programs read them. The ledger, the program that keeps each account's balance, reads them. It handles 8 payments a second, and 30 arrive. After an hour, it's 79,200 payments behind.

So the team starts two more copies of the ledger. For a few seconds, every payment waits while the three sort out who reads what. Afterwards, the logs show payments added twice.

It's easy to think more copies share the work the way more hands do. They do share it, but sharing takes agreement. Every time a copy joins or leaves, the work is handed around, and a careless handover stops work or repeats it.

In Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees, we built one consumer with one bookmark per partition. In this lesson, we'll start several, watch them split the work, hand bookmarks over cleanly, and find out what gets a member thrown out. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Three copies of the ledger share the `payments` topic, which Kafka splits into 6 partitions, separate logs that each keep their own order. They use Kafka 4.4's default settings. A fourth copy starts. While the four share the partitions out again, how many of the six stop being read?
options: Only the one or two partitions that move to the new copy
All six: by default, every copy hands back every partition before the new plan arrives
None: the sharing out happens in the background
Only the partitions of the busiest copy
warmup.why: With default settings, the client uses the classic protocol, the older set of rules for groups of consumers. Its default recipe for sharing out partitions is Range, which is eager: every member hands back all of its partitions before it rejoins, so the whole group stops. The first option is what the cooperative recipe and the new protocol (`group.protocol=consumer`) do, but you have to choose them. The third section shows all three.

sections.h: Sharing the work: a group gives each partition one owner
sections.body:
Let's start where the opening did, with one ledger that can't keep up. Each payment is a record in the Kafka topic `payments`, a named log. Kafka splits a topic into partitions, separate logs that each keep their own order. A record's place in its partition is its offset. A consumer, such as the ledger, reads a partition in order and saves a bookmark that says how far it got. Saving it is called committing, and the bookmark is the committed offset.

One ledger applies about 8 payments a second, because each one waits 120 ms for the card's bank to answer. At month-end, 30 payments arrive every second. A single ledger falls 22 payments further behind every second: 79,200 after an hour. We need four of them.

The simplest idea is to start four copies of the program. But every reader can read the whole topic (The log: Kafka's one big idea), so every payment would be applied four times. The next idea is to share records the way the queue in Queues and brokers did: competing consumers, where whoever is free takes the next message. That breaks two things we rely on. Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering put all of one account's records, such as acct-7's, in one partition, in order, so a refund never arrives before the payment it refunds. With two consumers on one partition, the refund could be applied first. And the bookmark is one number per partition, which only works if one reader moves it.

A restaurant has the same problem with its tables. If every waiter served every table, each table would get three desserts. If whoever was free grabbed the next dish, a main course could reach a table before its starter. So the manager gives each table to one waiter, and each waiter looks after several tables.

Kafka shares the work the same way. A **consumer group** is a set of consumers with the same `group.id`, here `ledger`. The group gives each partition to exactly one member, and a member can own several. With six partitions and three members, each member owns two (the figure calls the members c1, c2 and c3). Inside a partition, one reader keeps the order, as one waiter keeps a table's courses in order. And each partition still has one committed offset for the group.

You may have met this design before. Rebalancing and request routing, in the Partitioning track, called it fixed partitions. Split the keys into a fixed number of partitions once, keep a list of which owner has which partition, and move whole partitions when owners come and go. Kafka uses the design twice. Brokers, the computers that store the logs, own partitions for storage, and moving one to a new broker means copying its data. Members of a group own partitions for reading, and moving one copies nothing. The records stay on the brokers, and only the owner and the bookmark change hands. The list also lets a second group read everything. A group such as `fraud-check`, a program that looks for stolen cards, keeps its own list and its own bookmarks over the same partitions (figure).

Two things follow. A group can't use more members than it has partitions: a seventh member of a group on six partitions gets nothing and sits idle. And moving work around means moving partitions, which the rest of this lesson is about.

Who decides who owns what? One broker is the group's **coordinator**, the manager in our restaurant. It holds the group's bookmarks, in Kafka's own topic `__consumer_offsets`, and members tell it they're alive. An assignor is the recipe that turns "these members, these partitions" into a plan, called the assignment. There are three classic recipes. Range hands each member a block of partitions in a row, topic by topic. Round robin deals all the partitions out like cards. Sticky balances the group and moves as few partitions as possible. That's the Partitioning track's test of a good rebalancing scheme. When a member joins, move only its fair share, about 1/(N+1) of the partitions when there were N members, and move it only to the newcomer. The recipes differ more than you'd expect. With two topics of three partitions and two members, range gives one member four partitions and the other two, while round robin gives each three. The lab builds all three.

To join a group, a consumer sets `group.id` and calls `subscribe`, instead of `assign`, which would pick partitions by hand:

```java
var config = Map.<String, Object>of(
        "bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092",
        "group.id", "ledger",                 // the group: members share its partitions
        "group.protocol", "consumer",         // the new rebalance protocol (section 3)
        "enable.auto.commit", false,
        "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class,
        "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class);
var consumer = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(config);
consumer.subscribe(List.of("payments"));      // the group decides which partitions this member reads
```

```kotlin
val config = mapOf<String, Any>(
    "bootstrap.servers" to "localhost:9092",
    "group.id" to "ledger",                   // the group: members share its partitions
    "group.protocol" to "consumer",           // the new rebalance protocol (section 3)
    "enable.auto.commit" to false,
    "key.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
    "value.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
)
val consumer = KafkaConsumer<String, String>(config)
consumer.subscribe(listOf("payments"))        // the group decides which partitions this member reads
```

The two versions match line for line. The comment on `group.protocol` points ahead to the third section.

Splitting is the easy part. Next, we'll move a partition from one member to another, and see what happens to its bookmark.

try.title: Watch three consumers split six partitions
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the broker: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait`. Docker is a tool that runs programs in sealed boxes called containers, and this starts one Kafka broker in one.

Run `GroupDemo` (command below). It writes 10 payments to each partition of `ledger-rebalance`, a topic with 6 partitions. Then it starts three consumers of one new group, one after the other, on the new protocol. Each one prints what the group gives it and takes away. Before a partition leaves, a listener commits how far it got; the next section explains listeners.
Predict before you run it: when c3 joins, which partitions does it get, and does c1 stop reading the ones it keeps?

Describe the group it used (its name is on the first line of the output): `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group <name>`.

try.expect:
On a fresh broker:
```text
mode consumer, group ledger-consumer-1794084212193
  0.0s  c1 joins
  6.9s  c1 assigned [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], starts at [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], owns [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  7.1s  c2 joins
  8.0s  c1 revoked  [3, 4, 5], committed [10, 10, 10]
  8.8s  c2 assigned [3, 4, 5], starts at [10, 10, 10], owns [3, 4, 5]
  8.8s  c3 joins
  9.2s  c1 revoked  [2], committed [10]
  9.9s  c2 revoked  [5], committed [10]
 10.0s  c3 assigned [2], starts at [10], owns [2]
 11.0s  c3 assigned [5], starts at [10], owns [2, 5]
partitions handed back: {c1=4, c2=1}, 5 in all
records processed: 60, records in the topic: 60
```
Each new member took partitions only from what the others had too many of, and c1 kept 0 and 1 the whole time. c3 got 2 and 5 one at a time, as c1 and c2 let go of them. Every new owner started at 10, the offset its predecessor committed. The first assignment takes longer on a fresh broker (here 6.9 s), because the broker creates `__consumer_offsets` the first time it's needed; your times will differ. The describe (columns trimmed) shows the group's bookmarks after the demo closed it:

try.title: Take the handover away
steps: Keep the broker running. Run `GroupDemo` again with `nohandover` (command below). Now the listener doesn't commit when a partition leaves, and nothing else commits either.
Predict the last line: how many records will the group process, for how many records in the topic?

# or the Kotlin version:

try.expect:
Trimmed:
```text
mode consumer, group ledger-consumer-1794084252054, no handover commits
  1.8s  c1 assigned [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], starts at [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], owns [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  2.9s  c1 revoked  [3, 4, 5], committed nothing
  3.5s  c2 assigned [3, 4, 5], starts at [0, 0, 0], owns [3, 4, 5]
  4.2s  c1 revoked  [2], committed nothing
  4.7s  c2 revoked  [5], committed nothing
  4.8s  c3 assigned [2], starts at [0], owns [2]
  4.8s  c3 assigned [5], starts at [0], owns [2, 5]
records processed: 200, records in the topic: 120
```
The topic now holds 20 records per partition. c1 read all 120. Without a commit, the group's bookmark for partitions 3, 4 and 5 stayed empty, so c2 started at offset 0 (`auto.offset.reset=earliest`: start at the beginning when there's no bookmark) and read their 60 records again. c3 did the same for 2 and 5: 40 more. Five partitions moved, and 80 payments were processed twice, by nothing worse than adding two consumers.

sections.h: Three ways to move partitions, and what each one stops
sections.body:
How a group rebalances depends on the protocol it speaks, the set of rules its members and the coordinator follow. Kafka 4.4 has two.

The **classic protocol** works in rounds, like a manager who calls a staff meeting. When membership changes, the coordinator tells every member to rejoin, with a request called JoinGroup. It waits until all of them have, and picks one member as the group leader. That member runs the assignor. Then the coordinator sends each member its share, with SyncGroup. Two styles run on top of these rounds.

**Eager** is the original. A member rejoins empty-handed: before JoinGroup, it revokes every partition it owns. Nothing is processed until the new plan arrives, and a group of 100 members waits for the slowest of them. In the restaurant, every waiter leaves every table for the meeting. Frames 1 to 3 of the stepper show it. It's also what you get by default. The consumer's default `partition.assignment.strategy` is `[RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor]`, and the documentation says it uses Range, an eager assignor, until you remove Range from the list. By the Partitioning track's test, eager fails twice. It stops every partition, and it can move partitions between old members that didn't need to move.

**Cooperative** rebalancing keeps the rounds, but members keep their partitions while they rejoin. It came with Kafka 2.4, as KIP-429. (A KIP, a Kafka Improvement Proposal, is a written plan for a change to Kafka.) The assignor, `CooperativeStickyAssignor`, works out which partitions must move. Their owners revoke only those, and a second round hands them out. Nobody else stops, but every move costs two rounds.

The **new consumer group protocol**, KIP-848, has been ready for real use since Kafka 4.0, and it drops the rounds. Each member sends a heartbeat, a small "still here" message, every few seconds, and the coordinator answers it. The coordinator runs the assignor itself (`uniform` by default, or `range`) whenever membership changes, and keeps a target plan. Each member compares what it owns with its target and moves toward it on its own. First it revokes what it must give up, then the coordinator gives it what others have let go. There's no meeting for the whole group, members that keep their partitions never notice, and there's no leader to wait for. The manager walks round and taps only the waiters whose tables change. Frames 4 to 6 show it.

You must opt in. The broker side is on by default in Kafka 4.0 and later, but in 4.4 the client still defaults to `group.protocol=classic`. Set `group.protocol=consumer`. Three classic settings then belong to the broker instead: `session.timeout.ms`, `heartbeat.interval.ms` and `partition.assignment.strategy`. If you set one of them on the client, it throws a `ConfigException`, its error for a bad setting. The broker's `group.consumer.*` settings replace them, and `group.remote.assignor` picks the broker's assignor. You can move a group from classic to the new protocol by restarting its members one at a time, and the mixed group keeps working.

The new protocol has one cost. Plans travel on heartbeats, so a member hears about a change only at its next heartbeat, every 5 seconds by default (`group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms`). The lab broker uses 1 second, so the demos finish quickly.

Rebalances we start on purpose can be cheap now. Next, we'll look at the ones nobody asked for: when the group decides a member is gone.

frames.say: c3 asks to join. The coordinator tells every member to rejoin, and under the **eager** rules a member rejoins with nothing. c1 and c2 call `onPartitionsRevoked` with all their partitions, commit, and stop. For the next few seconds, no partition of `payments` is read, although only some of them will move.

refs.title: KIP-848: The next generation of the consumer rebalance protocol

sections.h: Two clocks decide when a member is gone
sections.body:
A rebalance also starts when the group decides a member is gone. It decides with two separate clocks, and they catch different failures.

The first clock checks that the program is alive. A background thread in the client sends heartbeats. If the coordinator hears nothing for the **session timeout**, 45 seconds by default, it removes the member and gives its partitions away. That catches a crash, a program stopped with `kill -9`, or a pulled network cable. It also means a crashed member's partitions sit unread for up to 45 seconds. A member that closes cleanly with `close()` leaves at once instead. On the classic protocol, the client settings `session.timeout.ms` and `heartbeat.interval.ms` (3 s) control this clock. On the new one, the broker's `group.consumer.session.timeout.ms` and `group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms` do.

The second clock checks that your loop is making progress. Heartbeats keep flowing even while your code is stuck waiting for the card's bank, so heartbeats alone can't catch that. If your code doesn't call `poll` again within `max.poll.interval.ms`, 5 minutes by default, the client leaves the group by itself. In `SlowConsumerDemo`, c1 has a 4-second limit, and one payment takes 8 seconds. At 4 seconds c1 leaves, and a second later c2 owns c1's partition and processes it from the last commit. When c1 comes back, it finishes the records it was holding, so they're processed twice. Its commit fails with `CommitFailedException`, and its next `poll` reports the partitions as lost and rejoins the group. The fix is the one from the last lesson: lower `max.poll.records` until a batch fits easily inside the limit.

Watch for the loop this can start. A member that's slow because its partitions are busy gets thrown out. Its partitions land on the others, which are now busier and slower, so they overrun the limit too. The group rebalances again and again, while its lag, how far behind it is, climbs. The Partitioning track warned about this kind of cascading failure: an overloaded machine declared dead, and its load moved onto the rest. Detecting failure: timeouts, heartbeats and gray failure explains why a slow member and a dead one look alike from outside. The fix is the same as there. Set the limit with room to spare over the slowest normal batch, not the average one.

Restarts are the third source of rebalances. Putting a new version of the ledger into use means stopping and starting each copy in turn. For six copies, that's six leaves and six joins: twelve rebalances in a few minutes, with partitions moving to another member and back. **Static membership** stops that. Give each copy a fixed name in `group.instance.id`, such as `ledger-3` for the third copy. A static member that shuts down keeps its partitions, and nobody else is disturbed. When a copy with the same name comes back within the session timeout, it gets the same partitions. In the restaurant, it's a waiter who steps out for a minute while their tables wait. The price: if it doesn't come back, its partitions wait the full session timeout before anyone takes them.

How do you see a group falling behind? With lag: for each partition, the offset where the log ends minus the group's committed offset. `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe` prints it for each partition. Lag that grows steadily means too few consumers or slow processing. Lag that jumps on every partition at once, again and again, usually means the group keeps rebalancing.

All these tools move partitions between members. None of them helps when one record in a partition fails every time it's read, and that's where the next lesson starts.

try.title: Stall a consumer, then restart one
steps: Run `SlowConsumerDemo` (command below). Two consumers share a new topic with 2 partitions. c1 has `max.poll.interval.ms=4000`, and pay-2 makes it wait 8 s for a card's bank that hangs.
Predict: who processes c1's partition while it waits, and what happens to c1's commit when it wakes up?

Then run `RestartDemo`, which stops c1 and starts it again 3 s later, as putting in a new version would. First run `./gradlew :kafka:demo -Pmain=sfz.msg.l08.demo.RestartDemo`, then the same command with `-Pargs=static` (or `RestartDemoKt` for Kotlin). Watch c2's lines.
Stop the broker and delete its data: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml down -v`.

`SlowConsumerDemo`:
```text

  3.0s  c1 assigned [1], starts at offset [0]
  3.6s  c1 partition 1: pay-2 calls the card issuer, which hangs for 8 s
  3.6s  c2 partition [0]: processed [pay-0, pay-1, pay-2, pay-3, pay-4]
```

About 4 s into the hang, c1 left, and c2 took partition 1 from offset 0 and processed all ten. c1 then finished pay-0 to pay-4 as well: five payments processed twice. Its commit was refused, the listener heard `onPartitionsLost`, and c1 rejoined. Which consumer gets which partition first varies between runs. `RestartDemo` without `static` (trimmed):

compare.title: A rebalance listener that hands the bookmark over, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin

compare.note: The same three functions in both. Java must override `onPartitionsLost` to stop the interface's default, which calls `onPartitionsRevoked` and would commit a partition that's no longer yours; Kotlin's override does the same job. Kotlin builds the map of offsets in one expression with `mapNotNull` and `toMap`, where Java fills a `HashMap` in a loop. Both keep `done` as a plain map, without locks: the consumer calls the listener on the polling thread, inside `poll`, so nothing else touches it at the same time.

Keep batches small enough that 100 payments at 120 ms (12 s) fit easily inside `max.poll.interval.ms`.

steps.say: Subscribe with the handover listener, and tell it about every payment once it's applied. The loop still commits after each batch, so a crash repeats at most one batch. The listener covers the moment a partition leaves between two commits.

Put it into use one copy at a time. KIP-848 supports this move while the group keeps running: during the switch the group holds members of both protocols, and the coordinator keeps it working. Watch it with `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group ledger --members`. Each member has an id and its partitions, and lag stays flat while a copy restarts.

Check the three ways a member can leave. A clean shutdown (`close()`) revokes and commits, and a static member's partitions wait for it until the session timeout. A crash repeats from the last batch commit, which the ledger's key check absorbs. A batch stuck past `max.poll.interval.ms` makes the member leave. Its later commit fails with `CommitFailedException`, and the listener gets `onPartitionsLost` and commits nothing. The lab's broker test grows a real group from one member to three, and checks that no payment is processed twice.

lab.title: Build the assignors and a handover listener, then grow a real group
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 16 fail. `AssignorsTest` and `StickyAssignorTest` need no broker. `HandoverListenerTest` drives your listener with `MockConsumer`, a pretend consumer in memory, whose `rebalance` and `losePartitions` methods play the coordinator. `RebalanceOnBrokerTest` runs a real group on a Kafka 4.4 broker, in Docker.
In `Assignors.java`, write `range` and `roundRobin`. Sort the members by id first, as Kafka does, and give every member an entry, even when it gets nothing.

In `StickyAssignor.kt`, write `assign`. Every member keeps what it owned, up to its quota: `partitions / members`, plus one for the first `partitions % members` members, with those extra slots going to the members that owned the most. Then deal the leftover partitions to whoever still has room. Then write `toRevoke`.

In `HandoverListener.kt`, write the four functions: remember each processed record's next offset, commit the revoked partitions' offsets, record every event, and on `onPartitionsLost`, forget without committing.

Run everything until all 16 pass. The broker test grows a group from one member to three, writing 60 records at each step, and checks that all 180 were processed exactly once. The poll loop never commits, so only your handover can make that true. The test runs once with `group.protocol=consumer` and once with the classic eager protocol, and checks what each one revoked.
hints: Range, for each topic: with `n` partitions and `m` members, member `i` starts at `i * (n / m) + min(i, n % m)` and takes `n / m` partitions, plus one if `i < n % m`.
For the sticky quotas, sort members by how many of their old partitions still exist, largest first, then by id. The first `partitions % members` of that order get the extra slot.
In the listener, build the commit map only from partitions you have an offset for, and skip `commitSync` when it's empty.

drill.title: The handover listener from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write a `ConsumerRebalanceListener` that commits the next offset to read for every revoked partition it has processed records from, and commits nothing for lost partitions. Then answer: under the new protocol, c4 joins a group in which c1, c2 and c3 own two partitions each of a topic with 6 partitions. How many partitions does each old member give up?

recap: A consumer group shares a topic by partition: each partition has exactly one owner in the group, and the group keeps one committed offset for it. Members beyond the number of partitions sit idle.
A rebalance moves partitions when members join or leave. Commit in `onPartitionsRevoked`, so the next owner starts exactly where you stopped; never commit in `onPartitionsLost`.
The default assignor list uses Range, which is eager: every member hands back everything on every rebalance. Cooperative rebalancing moves only what must move, in two rounds.

The new protocol (KIP-848, `group.protocol=consumer`) lets the broker work out the plan, and each member moves toward it on its own: revoke first, then assign. The 4.4 client still defaults to classic.
Heartbeats and the session timeout (45 s) catch dead programs; `max.poll.interval.ms` (5 minutes) catches stuck loops. Static membership (`group.instance.id`) keeps partitions through a restart.
The limit: one member reads each partition, in order. A record that fails every time it's read stops its partition, and no rebalance can move the work past it.
closing:
We started with a month-end rush, two new copies of the ledger, a few seconds when every payment waited, and payments added twice. The pause came from the eager default, which stops every partition to move a few. The repeats came from partitions that moved without a commit.

Next time you eat out at a change of shift, watch the tables. Does every table wait while the staff meet, as eager does? Or does each leaving waiter hand over only their own tables, with a word about what's been served, as the new protocol does?

Next, we'll meet a payment that no number of consumers can get past: a record that fails every time, and stops its whole partition.

quiz.q: From Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees: c1 commits after each batch of 500. It has applied 300 records of a batch from partition 4 when a rebalance moves partition 4 to c2. c1 has no rebalance listener. What does c2 do?
options: It starts after the 300, because the group tracks c1's progress
It starts at the last committed offset, so up to 300 records are applied a second time
It waits until c1 finishes the batch, then starts after it
It starts at the end of the log, so the rest of c1's batch is skipped
quiz.why: The new owner can only start where the group's bookmark is, and c1 last committed before this batch. Kafka knows nothing about c1's progress in memory: that's the position versus the committed offset. A commit in `onPartitionsRevoked` closes the gap. When it can't, as after a crash, the ledger's idempotency check makes the repeat harmless.

quiz.q: The ledger group on a topic with 20 partitions grows from 4 members to 5, with `group.protocol=consumer`. What does the rebalance move, compared with adding a fifth broker to store those partitions?
options: About 4 partitions' worth of records, copied to the new member's disk, just as for a new broker
All 20 partitions, because the plan is worked out again from scratch
Nothing until someone adds partitions to the topic
The ownership and committed offsets of about 4 partitions. No records are copied, while a new broker must copy every byte of the partitions it takes
quiz.why: A consumer group is fixed partitions applied to readers. A sticky plan moves the newcomer's fair share, 20 / 5 = 4 partitions, the smallest move possible, and the new owner starts reading at their committed offsets. The records never leave the brokers. A new broker is the storage side of the same scheme, so it must copy the data of every partition it takes over. Working the plan out from scratch is what eager rebalancing feels like, but even eager moves only ownership.

quiz.q: A group of three uses the classic protocol with `CooperativeStickyAssignor`. A fourth member joins. Which partitions stop being read during the rebalance?
options: All of them, until the new assignment arrives
None at all
Only the partitions that move to the new member, while they move
Only the partitions of the group leader
quiz.why: Cooperative rebalancing lets members keep their partitions while they rejoin. Only the owners of partitions that must move revoke them, and a second round hands them to the new member. The first option is eager rebalancing, which is what the default assignor list gives you.

quiz.q: A consumer's batches sometimes take 7 minutes, because a service it calls is slow. Its heartbeats are fine. With default settings, what happens?
options: After 5 minutes without a `poll`, the client leaves the group. Its partitions move, the new owner processes the batch again, and the old member's commit fails
Nothing: heartbeats prove it's alive
The session timeout runs out and the coordinator removes it
The broker slows down its fetches
quiz.why: Heartbeats only prove the program is running; `max.poll.interval.ms` (300,000 ms, which is 5 minutes) checks that the loop calls `poll`. Past it, the client leaves on its own. That causes a rebalance and repeated work, and the late commit fails with `CommitFailedException`. The fix is a smaller `max.poll.records` or faster processing, not a longer session timeout.

quiz.q: The ledger runs six copies with static membership (`group.instance.id`) and the default 45-second session timeout. The machine under one copy fails, and that copy never comes back. What happens to its partitions?
options: They move to the other members at once
They're not read for about 45 seconds, then the coordinator gives them to other members
They stay unread until the copy comes back
The whole group stops until someone removes the member by hand
quiz.why: A static member's partitions are kept for it until the session timeout passes, because it might be restarting. That's what makes putting in a new version cheap, and it's the price here: the partitions wait out the full timeout, and lag builds on them. Then the coordinator removes the member and shares its partitions out among the others.

flashcards.front: How does a consumer group share a topic?
flashcards.back: By partition: each partition has exactly one owner in the group at a time, and the group keeps one committed offset for each partition.

flashcards.front: What does the default classic `partition.assignment.strategy` do in a rebalance?
flashcards.back: It's `[RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor]` and uses Range, which is eager: every member hands back all its partitions first.

flashcards.front: How do you opt in to the KIP-848 protocol, and what must you remove?
flashcards.back: Set `group.protocol=consumer`. Remove `session.timeout.ms`, `heartbeat.interval.ms` and `partition.assignment.strategy`: the client refuses them.

flashcards.front: What should `onPartitionsRevoked` do, and what must `onPartitionsLost` not do?
flashcards.back: Revoked: commit the next offset to read for each partition you processed. Lost: don't commit, because the partitions already belong to someone else.

flashcards.front: Which failure does `max.poll.interval.ms` catch that heartbeats can't?
flashcards.back: A loop that's stuck or too slow. Heartbeats come from a background thread, so they keep flowing. The default is 5 minutes.
The member becomes static: a restart within the session timeout gets the same partitions back, without a rebalance.

flashcards.front: A partition moves to a new broker, or to a new member of a consumer group. What moves in each case?
flashcards.back: To a broker: the data, copied byte by byte. To a group member: only the ownership and the committed offset; the records stay on the brokers.

terms.plain: Consumers with the same `group.id` that share a topic's partitions: one owner per partition, and one committed offset per partition.
The broker that manages a group's members and stores its committed offsets.
The recipe that decides which member gets which partition: range, round robin, sticky, or the broker's `uniform`.
Moving partitions between members because a member joined, left or was thrown out.
Every member hands back all its partitions before the new plan arrives, so the whole group stops.
Members keep their partitions during a rebalance and hand back only the ones that move.
Functions the consumer calls inside `poll` when partitions are assigned, revoked or lost.
A member with a fixed `group.instance.id`, whose partitions wait for it during a restart.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why every time a new version of the ledger goes out, lag jumps on all partitions and a few repeated payments show up in the logs. Explain what happens while the new version goes out, and what you'd change.
explain_back.answer: We put a new version out by restarting the copies one at a time. Each copy that stops leaves the group, and each copy that starts joins it, so every step causes a rebalance. We run the classic protocol with the default assignor, which is eager. In every rebalance, every member hands back all of its partitions and waits for the new plan, so all partitions stop at once. That's the jump in lag. The repeats come from the handover. Our consumer commits after each batch but not in `onPartitionsRevoked`, so a partition that moves starts again at the last batch commit, and the new owner applies what the old owner had already done. The idempotency check catches them, which is why we only see them in the logs. I'd switch to `group.protocol=consumer`, so only the partitions that move pause. I'd add a rebalance listener that commits processed offsets when partitions are revoked, and commits nothing when they're lost. And I'd give each copy a fixed `group.instance.id`, such as `ledger-3`, so a restarting copy keeps its partitions and nothing moves at all.

deeper.body:
**Epochs keep the new protocol honest.** KIP-848 keeps three counters. The group epoch goes up whenever members or their subscriptions change. The target plan carries the epoch it was worked out for. Each member has a member epoch, and it moves up only once that member has caught up with the target. A heartbeat or commit from a member with an old epoch is refused with `FENCED_MEMBER_EPOCH`. That's how the coordinator stops a member that missed a change from acting on partitions it no longer owns.

**Pattern subscriptions moved to the broker.** With the new protocol, `subscribe(SubscriptionPattern)` sends a pattern of topic names (an RE2/J regular expression) to the coordinator, which matches it against the cluster's topics. A new topic that matches is picked up without every client asking the brokers for the list of topics. Only the new protocol supports it.

**Range still matters for joins.** Say two topics are split the same way: `payments` and `refunds`, both keyed by account, both with 12 partitions. Range gives partition 3 of both to the same member, so one consumer sees an account's payments and its refunds and can match them up locally. The broker's `range` assignor keeps that property; set `group.remote.assignor=range` to get it. The lab's test that one member gets the extra partition of every topic is the same property seen from the other side.

**Share groups are a different tool.** Share groups and running Kafka in production covers share groups, where several members read the same partition and each record is acknowledged on its own. They give up the order within a partition to allow more consumers than partitions.
